echoes.note: The command to give generously to the poor ('open wide your hand to your brother') is the Torah background for Jesus' presupposition that disciples 'do merciful deeds'; almsgiving is assumed righteousness, not optional.
'Whoever is kind to the poor lends to the LORD, and he will repay him' — the logic of God himself repaying the secret almsgiver (v.4) closely matches this proverb's reward-from-God motif.

Ben Sira: a person's almsgiving is 'like a signet ring' kept with God who guards it as a treasure — Second Temple development of almsgiving stored with God who rewards, paralleling the Father who sees in secret.

Tobit's instruction to give alms from one's substance, that almsgiving 'delivers from death' and 'stores up a good treasure,' is the closest Second Temple parallel to Jesus' theology of hidden, God-rewarded charity.

'Prayer with fasting and almsgiving... is better than to lay up gold' and 'almsgiving saves from death' — the same triad of almsgiving/prayer/fasting that structures Mt 6:1-18, suggesting a shared piety pattern.
Isaiah's true fast as sharing bread with the hungry links almsgiving and fasting as authentic versus performative piety, the very contrast Jesus draws.
Elisha 'shut the door' and prayed to the LORD in private before raising the child — a possible OT precedent for entering one's room and shutting the door (v.6) to pray unseen.

'Enter your chambers, and shut your doors behind you' — striking verbal overlap with 'enter into your inner room, and having shut your door,' though the contexts differ (hiding from wrath vs. private prayer).
The prophets of Baal cried aloud 'from morning until noon' with no answer — a possible backdrop for the Gentiles' 'much speaking' (v.7) imagining they are heard for many words.
'Let your words be few' before God in heaven — a wisdom warning against verbose prayer that closely matches the rebuke of 'vain repetitions' and 'much speaking.'
'Do not babble in the assembly of the elders, and do not repeat yourself in your prayer' — almost a direct Second Temple parallel to the warning against vain repetition.
God knows the word on the tongue before it is spoken — grounds Jesus' claim that 'your Father knows what things you need, before you ask him' (v.8).

'I will sanctify my great name... and the nations will know that I am the LORD' — the divine self-hallowing of God's name is the OT engine behind 'hallowed be your name'; God hallows his name by his eschatological act, which the petition invokes.
'They will sanctify my name... and stand in awe of the God of Israel' — sanctifying/hallowing the divine Name as eschatological hope, the conceptual root of the first petition.
'You shall not profane my holy name, but I will be hallowed among the children of Israel' — the covenantal duty to hallow the Name underlies 'hallowed be your name.'
'The God of heaven will set up a kingdom which will never be destroyed' — the prayer 'Let your Kingdom come' draws directly on Daniel's vision of God's everlasting kingdom breaking into history.
'Your God reigns!' — the proclamation of God's kingship/reign that 'your Kingdom come' petitions to be realized.
'And the kingdom will be the LORD's' — terse OT articulation of the coming divine kingdom echoed in the second petition.
'As may be the will in heaven, so let him do' — a Second Temple formula of submission to heaven's will closely paralleling 'your will be done.'
The heavenly hosts 'do his will' (v.20-21) — the angelic obedience in heaven is the model for 'your will be done, as in heaven, so on earth.'
'Whatever the LORD pleased, that he has done, in heaven and in earth' — the heaven/earth scope of God's will echoes in the third petition's cosmic frame.

'Feed me with the food that is needful for me' (Agur's prayer for neither poverty nor riches, just the daily portion) — the closest OT analogue to 'Give us today our daily bread,' both asking for sufficient daily provision.
The manna gathered 'a day's portion every day' is the typological pattern for daily bread: God provides enough for today, teaching dependence rather than hoarding (cf. anxiety section vv.25-34).
The manna could not be stored overnight without rotting — reinforces the day-by-day reliance behind 'give us today our daily bread' and against laying up earthly treasure.

'Forgive your neighbor the wrong he has done, and then your sins will be pardoned when you pray' — a remarkably close Second Temple parallel to the reciprocal forgiveness of the fifth petition and vv.14-15.
The sabbatical 'release' (remission) of debts colors 'forgive us our debts' — debt-remission language drawn from Torah jubilee/release practice applied to sins.
'Blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered' — the divine forgiveness of sin/debt sought in 'forgive us our debts.'
Petitions for God to deliver from the enemy/evildoer underlie 'deliver us from the evil one'; the Psalter's deliverance language saturates the final petition.
'Incline not my heart to any evil thing' — a prayer not to be led toward evil that parallels 'bring us not into temptation.'

'Yours, O LORD, is the greatness, the power... the kingdom... and the glory' — David's doxology is the verbatim source of the prayer's traditional closing ascription of kingdom, power, and glory to God.
David asks God to keep his people's hearts directed toward him — continues the doxological context (29:11) from which the Lord's Prayer ending is drawn.

'Forgive your neighbor... and then your sins will be pardoned'; the wrathful man who holds anger cannot expect healing from God — the strongest Second Temple statement of conditional, reciprocal forgiveness mirroring vv.14-15.
'You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge... but you shall love your neighbor' — the Torah ground for releasing others' trespasses as a condition of one's own standing before God.
Joseph's brothers beg him to forgive their trespass and Joseph forgives — a narrative model of human forgiveness as the channel of restored relationship.
Wrath and anger are abominations that the sinner holds tight, and 'the Lord will take vengeance' on the unforgiving — the immediate context preceding the forgiveness teaching of Sir 28:2.

Isaiah's polemic against fasting done for show ('to be heard on high'... bowing the head like a reed) versus the fast God chooses — the prophetic template for Jesus' contrast between hypocritical and hidden fasting.
'Rend your heart, and not your garments' — true fasting is inward not performative, the same heart-versus-display contrast Jesus presses against disfigured faces.
'When you fasted... did you at all fast to me, even to me?' — God's challenge that ritual fasting may be self-directed rather than God-directed, paralleling fasting 'to be seen by men.'
'Wash yourself, anoint yourself' — anointing and washing as ordinary grooming (the opposite of mourning), the gesture Jesus prescribes to mask fasting (v.17).
David washes and anoints himself when he ceases mourning — the cultural background for anointing the head and washing the face to appear un-fasting.
The triad 'prayer with fasting and almsgiving' commends fasting as genuine piety, paralleling the assumed practice of fasting that Jesus purifies of display.
Daniel mourns and does NOT anoint himself while fasting — the very mourning-fast convention Jesus reverses by telling disciples to anoint themselves.

'Lay up your treasure according to the commandments... store up almsgiving in your treasuries, and it will rescue you from every misfortune' — the most direct Second Temple parallel to laying up treasure in heaven through righteous use of wealth.
'Don't weary yourself to be rich... riches sprout wings like an eagle and fly away' — the transience of earthly wealth behind 'treasures on earth, where... thieves break through and steal.'
The wicked heaps up silver like dust but the just will wear it — the futility of hoarded wealth that another takes, echoing treasure consumed or stolen.
The rich man 'carries nothing away' at death; his glory does not descend with him — undergirds the worthlessness of earthly treasure.
Riches kept by their owner to his hurt, perishing by misfortune, leaving nothing in hand — Qoheleth's meditation on perishable wealth.
Almsgiving lays up 'a good treasure for yourself against the day of necessity' — explicit treasure-storing-with-God language behind treasures in heaven.
Bringing tithes into God's storehouse so that heaven's windows pour out blessing — a heaven-versus-earth economy of giving that resonates faintly with heavenly treasure.
Kindness to the poor 'lends to the LORD' who repays — the mechanism by which earthly generosity becomes heavenly treasure.

'He who has a generous eye (bountiful eye) will be blessed' — the Hebrew idiom of the 'good/generous eye' versus the stingy eye underlies the 'sound' (single) eye and the 'evil eye,' linking the lamp saying to generosity (cf. surrounding treasure/mammon).
'A man with an evil eye hastens after riches' — the 'evil eye' as greed/stinginess, the very vice contrasted with the sound eye between the treasure and mammon sayings.
Warning against a 'wicked' (mean/evil) eye toward the needy brother — the evil eye as ungenerous miserliness, contextually fitting the eye/lamp logion's placement amid wealth teaching.
'The commandment is a lamp... the way of life' — light/lamp as moral illumination, the metaphor field Jesus uses for the eye as the body's lamp.
'Your word is a lamp to my feet' — lamp/light as inner moral guidance, the imagery undergirding the eye as the lamp of the body.
'An evil eye is grudging of bread' — Ben Sira's stingy 'evil eye' that begrudges sharing, fitting the generosity reading of the evil eye versus sound eye.
'The spirit of man is the LORD's lamp, searching all his innermost parts' — inner illumination imagery related to the lamp of the body.
'Love the LORD your God with all your heart' — the Shema's demand of undivided love is what divided service to two masters (God and Mammon) violates; one cannot love both wholly.
'Choose this day whom you will serve' — the exclusive either/or of covenant allegiance behind 'no one can serve two masters.'
'How long will you waver between two opinions?' — Elijah's demand to choose between the LORD and Baal, the prophetic either/or pattern of single-master service.
'You shall have no other gods before me' — making wealth a rival master is functional idolatry, the first commandment's exclusivity reframed as God versus Mammon.
The lover of gold cannot be justified; gold has been a stumbling block and ruin to many — Ben Sira on wealth as an idol-like snare, paralleling serving Mammon.
'Cast your burden on the LORD, and he will sustain you' — the antidote to anxiety is entrusting provision to God, the heart of 'don't be anxious for your life.'
'I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his children begging bread' — God's reliable provision for the righteous undergirds 'your heavenly Father feeds them... how much more you.'
God brings forth food and 'satisfies' creation — the Creator's provision for plants, beasts, and people grounds the argument from birds and lilies to human care.
'These all wait for you... you give them their food in due season' — God feeds all creatures, directly behind 'your heavenly Father feeds' the birds.
'He gives to the animals their food, and to the young ravens which cry' — God feeding the birds is the precise image of 'See the birds of the sky... your heavenly Father feeds them.'
'Who provides for the raven its prey, when its young ones cry?' — the divine-speech argument that God feeds wild birds, paralleling the lesson of v.26.
'Ask the animals... the birds of the sky' — they teach that God's hand holds all life; the pedagogy of learning providence from birds matches 'See the birds of the sky.'
Ravens feed Elijah at God's command — a narrative enactment of God using birds in provision, faintly behind the birds-fed-by-the-Father motif.
Solomon's surpassing glory and splendor (the queen of Sheba's awe) is the explicit comparison: 'even Solomon in all his glory was not dressed like one of these' (v.29).
The daily manna ('a day's portion') typifies the day-at-a-time trust of 'don't be anxious for tomorrow'; Israel's wilderness schooling in non-hoarding dependence.
God let Israel hunger then fed with manna 'that he might teach you that man does not live by bread alone' — provision as a lesson in dependence, behind seeking the Kingdom first over food.
Solomon seeks wisdom (God's priority) and is given riches and honor 'as well' — the exact pattern of 'seek first God's Kingdom... and all these things will be added.'
'Commit your works to the LORD, and your plans will be established' — entrusting one's concerns to God rather than anxious self-provision.
'All flesh is grass... the grass withers' — the transience of grass that today is and tomorrow is burned (v.30) draws on Isaiah's grass-and-flower imagery of human frailty.
Humanity 'like grass which grows up. In the morning it flourishes... in the evening it is cut down' — the grass-of-the-field's day-long life behind v.30.
'As for man, his days are like grass... the wind passes over it, and it is gone' — reinforces the perishable grass imagery applied to the field's clothing.
Toil for bread and the field's produce under the curse — the labor of sowing/reaping and anxious provision that Jesus relativizes by pointing to birds that neither sow nor reap.

Manna provision teaches that 'it is not the production of crops that feeds humankind but your word that sustains those who trust in you' — Second Temple reflection on God-given sustenance versus anxious labor.
'Anxiety brings on premature old age' — Ben Sira on the harm of worry, faintly paralleling 'which of you by being anxious can add to his lifespan?'
The ant gathers in summer — a nature-observation wisdom form ('consider the ant'); Jesus inverts the genre with 'consider the lilies' which do NOT toil, yet are clothed.
